questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a spherical mirror?
questions.a: Its reflecting surface is curved, shaped like a part of a hollow sphere
o: Its reflecting surface is curved, shaped like a part of a hollow sphere
Its reflecting surface is flat, but its outline is a circle
It always forms an erect image of the same size as the object
It is any shiny surface that shows an upside-down image

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I: 1. Inner side of a shiny spoon, 2. Outer side of a shiny spoon, 3. Plane mirror, 4. Non-reflecting surface in a mirror diagram
Column II: A. Shown shaded, B. Image looks inverted, C. Image is erect but smaller, D. Image is erect and of the same size

Read these statements about spherical mirrors.
I. To make a concave mirror, the reflective coating is applied on the inner curved surface.
II. In the diagram of a mirror, the non-reflecting surface is shown shaded.
III. A thin layer of aluminium can be used as the reflective coating of a spherical mirror.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
III only
I, II and III

questions.q: In a science-lab cupboard, two spherical mirrors, X and Y, lie on a shelf with their shiny reflecting surfaces facing up. Seen from the side at eye level, the shiny surface of X sinks in at the middle like a saucer, while the shiny surface of Y bulges up at the middle like an upturned saucer. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: X is concave and Y is convex, so only X can show a far-away object upside down
o: X is concave and Y is convex, so only X can show a far-away object upside down
X is concave and Y is convex, so only Y can show a far-away object upside down
X is convex and Y is concave, so only Y can show a far-away object upside down
X is convex and Y is concave, so only X can show a far-away object upside down

questions.q: (a) What is a convex mirror? (b) Which side of a shiny metallic spoon behaves like a convex mirror?
questions.a: (a) A convex mirror is a spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves outwards. (b) The outer side of the spoon, which bulges outwards (it shows an erect but smaller image).
s: Defines a convex mirror as a spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves outwards
Names the outer, bulging side of the spoon

questions.q: True or false? 'The reflecting surface of a convex mirror curves inwards, like the inside of a bowl.' Give a reason or write the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The reflecting surface of a convex mirror curves outwards. A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves inwards, like the inside of a bowl, is a concave mirror.
s: States False
Corrects it: a convex mirror's reflecting surface curves outwards; curving inwards is a concave mirror

questions.q: A school laboratory receives a box labelled 'Spherical mirrors: 2 pieces'. (a) Each mirror can be thought of as a part of what shape? (b) Each mirror was made from a flat piece of glass. What was done to the flat glass to give it a curved surface? (c) What is the name of the piece whose reflecting surface curves inwards?
questions.a: (a) A part of a hollow (imaginary) sphere. (b) The flat glass was ground and polished into a curved surface (and then given a reflective coating). (c) A concave mirror.
s: States a part of a hollow sphere
States that the flat glass is ground and polished into a curved surface
Names the concave mirror

questions.q: Tanu makes two statements. Statement 1: 'The shiny steel spoon in my kitchen is not a spherical mirror specially made in a factory.' Statement 2: 'Its inner side and its outer side show my face in exactly the same way.' Check each statement. Is Tanu right, wrong or partly right?
questions.a: Partly right. Statement 1 is right: the spoon is just a curved shiny surface that acts like a mirror; curved mirrors such as spherical mirrors can also be specially made. Statement 2 is wrong: the inner side curves inwards and shows her face inverted, while the outer side bulges outwards and shows her face erect but smaller.
s: Verdict partly right: Statement 1 is correct, the spoon is a curved shiny surface, not a specially made mirror
Statement 2 is wrong: the inner side curves inwards and shows the face inverted
The outer side bulges outwards and shows the face erect but smaller

questions.q: At a hardware shop in Indore, two round spherical mirrors, P and Q, are fixed flat against a wall, so Ravi cannot look at them from the side. He holds his key ring about 3 cm in front of each. In P the key ring looks erect and larger than it is; in Q it looks erect and smaller. (a) Name each mirror and give the reason. (b) Does the reflecting surface of each mirror curve inwards or outwards? (c) A bus parked far away across the road is also seen in both mirrors. Predict how the bus looks in each. (d) Ravi's friend says: 'Both images were erect, so the two mirrors could just be plane mirrors.' Use Ravi's observations to show she is wrong.
questions.a: (a) P is a concave mirror, because an object close to a concave mirror gives an erect, enlarged image. Q is a convex mirror, because a convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished image. (b) P's reflecting surface curves inwards; Q's curves outwards. (c) In P (concave) the far-away bus looks inverted (and smaller); in Q (convex) it looks erect and diminished. (d) A plane mirror always gives an erect image of the same size as the object. P's image was larger and Q's was smaller, so neither can be a plane mirror.
s: (a) P concave (close object gives erect, enlarged image); Q convex (always erect, diminished)
(b) P curves inwards, Q curves outwards
(c) Bus inverted in P, erect and diminished in Q
(d) A plane mirror gives a same-size image; P's was larger and Q's smaller, so neither is plane

questions.q: A science teacher in Kochi has one curved glass piece, already ground and polished, and enough aluminium to coat only one of its two curved surfaces. She wants the finished mirror for two lessons. Lesson 1 needs an erect, enlarged view of a small object held close, the way a dentist's mirror works. Lesson 2 needs an image that turns upside down when the object is far away. Her assistant says: 'Coat the inner curved surface; both lessons will work either way.' (a) Decide which curved surface she should coat, and show that this one choice meets both lessons. (b) Judge the assistant's plan: name the mirror it would make and say what happens in each lesson. (c) After coating, describe one check, without using any object, that confirms she coated the right surface.
questions.a: (a) She needs a concave mirror, because only a concave mirror gives an erect, enlarged image of an object held close (Lesson 1) and an inverted image when the object is moved far away (Lesson 2). A concave mirror is formed when the coating is applied on the outer curved surface, so she should coat the outer surface. (b) The plan is wrong. Coating the inner curved surface makes a convex mirror. It always gives an erect, diminished image, so in Lesson 1 the object looks smaller, not enlarged, and in Lesson 2 the image never turns upside down. Both lessons fail. (c) Place the mirror with its reflecting surface facing up and view it from the side at eye level: the reflecting surface should be seen curving inwards.
s: (a) Both lessons need a concave mirror: erect, enlarged when close and inverted when far
(a) A concave mirror needs the coating on the outer curved surface
(b) Inner coating makes a convex mirror
(b) Convex image is always erect and diminished, so Lesson 1 gets no enlargement and Lesson 2 no inversion
(c) Side view at eye level shows the reflecting surface curving inwards

questions.q: Which of these uses a concave mirror?
questions.a: The reflector behind a scooter's headlight bulb
o: The reflector behind a scooter's headlight bulb
The side-view mirror fixed on a scooter's handle
The mirror fixed at a sharp bend in a hill road
The mirror that watches the aisles of a big store

questions.q: Megha's small hand mirror shows her face erect and larger than it really is when she holds it close. When she holds it at arm's length, her face looks upside down. What kind of mirror is it?
questions.a: A concave mirror
o: A concave mirror
A convex mirror
A plane mirror
A convex mirror when close, a concave one when far

questions.q:
Match each mirror in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Dentist's mirror, 2. Side-view mirror of a bus, 3. Main mirror of a modern reflecting telescope, 4. Mirror high in a corner of a big store
Column II: A. Convex; lets one person watch a large area to deter thefts, B. Concave; gives an enlarged view when held close, C. Convex; gives an erect, smaller image of the traffic behind, D. A large concave mirror
A mirror is known to be plane, concave or convex. Which single observation is enough on its own to show that it is concave?
questions.a: The image of a far-away object is inverted
o: The image of a far-away object is inverted
The image of the object is erect at every distance
The image is smaller than the object itself
The image shows lateral inversion, left for right

questions.q: (a) What is meant by a 'diminished' image? (b) Name the spherical mirror that always forms a diminished image.
questions.a: (a) A diminished image is smaller than the object. (b) A convex mirror (its image is always erect and diminished).
s: States that a diminished image is smaller than the object
Names the convex mirror

questions.q: (a) A shopkeeper fixes one mirror high in a corner of his big store so that, from the counter, he can watch the whole floor. Which type of spherical mirror should it be, and what makes it suitable? (b) His son suggests a large concave mirror instead, 'because it makes things look bigger'. Give one reason why a concave mirror would not do this job well.
questions.a: (a) A convex mirror. It is curved outwards, so it shows a much wider (large) area, and its image is always erect, so he can monitor the whole store. (b) Customers far from a concave mirror would be seen inverted (upside down) and getting smaller; a concave mirror gives an erect, enlarged image only when the object is close to it.
s: (a) Convex mirror, because its outward curve shows a much wider area with an erect image
(b) A concave mirror shows far-away customers inverted; it enlarges only objects close to it

questions.q: A tall tree far away is seen in each of three mirrors standing side by side: a plane mirror, a concave mirror and a convex mirror. (a) In which mirror does the tree look upside down? (b) In which mirror is the tree's image erect and of the same size as the object? (c) In which mirror is the tree's image erect but diminished?
questions.a: (a) The concave mirror (for a far object its image is inverted). (b) The plane mirror. (c) The convex mirror.
s: (a) Names the concave mirror
(b) Names the plane mirror
(c) Names the convex mirror

questions.q: Isha says: 'The convex mirror at a sharp bend on a hill road helps only the drivers coming from one side, and it works by showing the other vehicles larger than they are so that drivers notice them.' Check both parts of her claim. Is she right, wrong or partly right?
questions.a: Wrong, in both parts. A convex mirror at a road bend gives drivers from both sides the visibility of the other side, which helps prevent collisions. It does not show vehicles larger: a convex mirror always forms an erect image that is smaller than the actual vehicle. It helps because, being curved outwards, it shows a much wider area of the road.
s: Verdict wrong: the mirror helps drivers from both sides see the other side
The convex mirror's image is erect and smaller than the vehicle, not larger
It helps because its outward curve shows a much wider area of the road

questions.q:
A bus company in Lucknow must choose one kind of side-view mirror, plane or convex, of the same size, for its school buses. In a depot test (illustrative results), drivers did 10 trials with each mirror. With the plane mirror, a driver misjudged the gap to the car behind in 1 trial and failed to notice a scooter in the next lane in 4 trials. With the convex mirror, a driver misjudged the gap in 3 trials and failed to notice the scooter in 0 trials. A parent wants plane mirrors 'because they show cars at their real size'. The company will choose the mirror with fewer total mistakes.
(a) Why were gaps misjudged more often with the convex mirror?
(b) Why was the scooter missed more often with the plane mirror?
(c) Find the total number of mistakes for each mirror.
(d) Which mirror should the company fit? Justify your decision, and say what the data shows about the parent's point.
questions.a: (a) A convex mirror always forms an erect image that is smaller than the actual vehicle, so cars behind look smaller than they really are and drivers can misjudge them. A plane mirror shows them at the same size. (b) The convex mirror is curved outwards, so it shows a much wider area of the road behind; the plane mirror shows a narrower area, so a scooter in the next lane can be out of view. (c) Plane mirror: 1 + 4 = 5 mistakes. Convex mirror: 3 + 0 = 3 mistakes. (d) The convex mirror, since it gives fewer total mistakes (3 against 5). The data supports the parent on one point: with the plane mirror the gap was misjudged less often (1 against 3) because cars appear at their real size. But the plane mirror missed the scooter 4 times, so overall the convex mirror is safer; drivers should remember that cars in it look smaller than they are.
s: (a) The convex image is erect but smaller than the actual car, so gaps are misjudged
(b) The convex mirror's outward curve shows a much wider area; the plane mirror misses the next lane
(c) Plane 1 + 4 = 5 mistakes; convex 3 + 0 = 3 mistakes
(d) Chooses the convex mirror (3 < 5), granting the parent's point on gap-judging (1 < 3)

questions.q: A small toy is placed in front of a mirror and moved away step by step. Describe the image, saying whether it is erect or inverted and whether it is enlarged or diminished, in each case. (a) The toy is very close to a concave mirror. (b) The toy is moved farther from the concave mirror, just past where the image first turns over. (c) The toy is moved much farther from the concave mirror. (d) The toy is very close to a convex mirror. (e) The toy is moved far from the convex mirror.
questions.a: (a) Erect and enlarged. (b) Inverted and still enlarged. (c) Inverted and getting smaller (diminished). (d) Erect and diminished. (e) Still erect and diminished, only slightly smaller than before.
s: (a) Erect and enlarged
(b) Inverted and enlarged
(c) Inverted and getting smaller
(d) Erect and diminished
(e) Erect, diminished and only slightly smaller

questions.q: A thin beam of light falls on a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 47 degrees. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.a: 47 degrees
o: 47 degrees
43 degrees
94 degrees
133 degrees

questions.q: In ray diagrams, light is drawn as straight lines with arrows, called rays. Why is this a fair way to show light?
questions.a: Light travels along a straight line, and the arrow shows its direction
o: Light travels along a straight line, and the arrow shows its direction
Light always bends at a mirror, and the arrow shows the point where it bends
The length of each line shows how bright the light is at that place
The arrow marks the point at which the light finally stops travelling

questions.q: More than 800 years ago, during the time of the mathematician Bhaskara II, how did astronomers observe the positions of stars and planets?
questions.a: By viewing their reflected images in shallow bowls of water through tubes
o: By viewing their reflected images in shallow bowls of water through tubes
By focusing their light onto sheets of paper with large concave mirrors
By viewing them through curved drops of water placed on oiled glass strips
By catching their light on a bent sheet of paper beside a plane mirror

questions.q: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror so that the angle between the incident ray and the surface of the mirror is 62 degrees. What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray?
questions.a: 56 degrees
o: 56 degrees
62 degrees
28 degrees
124 degrees

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When a ray of light falls on a mirror along the normal, the angle of reflection is zero.
Reason (R): The angle of reflection is the angle between the reflected ray and the surface of the mirror.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is meant by the normal to a mirror at the point of incidence? (b) A ray makes an angle of 18 degrees with the normal before it strikes a plane mirror. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.a: (a) The normal is the line drawn at 90 degrees to the mirror at the point where the incident ray strikes it. (b) 18 degrees, because the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
s: Defines the normal as the line at 90 degrees to the mirror at the point of incidence
Gives the angle of reflection as 18 degrees

questions.q: True or false? 'The laws of reflection hold for concave and convex mirrors, just as they do for a plane mirror.' Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The laws of reflection are valid for all kinds of mirrors, plane and spherical. Even on a curved mirror, each ray of light follows the laws of reflection at the point where it strikes the surface.
s: States True
Reason: the laws are valid for all mirrors; each ray on a curved mirror still obeys them

questions.q: (a) State the law of reflection that links the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection. (b) State the other law of reflection, about the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray. (c) In the activity where a stiff chart-paper sheet under the mirror extends beyond the edge of the table, what happens to the reflected beam on the extended part when that part is bent down along the table's edge?
questions.a: (a) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. (b) The incident ray, the normal to the mirror at the point of incidence and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane. (c) The reflected beam disappears from the bent part (it reappears when the sheet is flattened again), because bending the sheet creates a new plane.
s: (a) Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection
(b) Incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie in the same plane
(c) The reflected beam is no longer seen on the bent part (reappears when flattened)

questions.q: A ray of light falls on a plane mirror, and the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is 108 degrees. (a) Find the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection. (b) Find the angle that the reflected ray makes with the surface of the mirror. (c) Teena says: 'If the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray were 0 degrees, the ray must have fallen along the normal.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The normal splits the 108 degrees into two equal angles, since the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection: 108 / 2 = 54 degrees each. (b) The normal is at 90 degrees to the mirror, so the reflected ray makes 90 - 54 = 36 degrees with the surface. (c) Yes. An angle of 0 degrees between the rays means the reflected ray goes back along the incident ray, so the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are both 0 degrees, which happens only when the ray falls along the normal.
s: (a) Halves 108 to get i = r = 54 degrees
(b) Finds 90 - 54 = 36 degrees with the mirror
(c) Agrees: 0 degrees between the rays means i = r = 0, so the ray is along the normal

questions.q: Sana does the plane-mirror activity with a torch, a comb slit and a protractor, and fills in her table. (a) The angle of incidence is 15 degrees. What angle of reflection should she find? (b) The beam falls along the normal. What are the two angles? (c) The angle of reflection is 71 degrees. What was the angle of incidence? (d) Name the law of reflection she used in all three answers.
questions.a: (a) 15 degrees. (b) Both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are 0 degrees. (c) 71 degrees. (d) The law that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
s: (a) 15 degrees
(b) Both angles 0 degrees
(c) 71 degrees
(d) Names the law: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection

questions.q:
For their school's annual day in Kochi, a Class 8 team wants a thin beam from a torch with a comb slit to bounce off a plane mirror and land on a paper star. They first try it on a sheet of white chart paper on a table, with part of the sheet hanging over the table's edge. The beam strikes the mirror with an angle of incidence of 42 degrees. The paper star is stuck on the part of the sheet that hangs over the edge, and that part is bent downwards along the edge.
(a) What is the angle of reflection?
(b) What is the angle between the incident beam and the reflected beam?
(c) Will the reflected beam be seen on the star while that part of the sheet is bent down? Explain using a law of reflection.
(d) The team now wants the angle between the incident and reflected beams to be 64 degrees. Should they increase or decrease the angle of incidence, and by how many degrees? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) 42 degrees. (b) 42 + 42 = 84 degrees. (c) No. The incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane; bending the sheet creates a new plane, so the reflected beam does not appear on the bent part until the sheet is flattened. (d) The angle of incidence must be 64 / 2 = 32 degrees, so they should decrease it by 42 - 32 = 10 degrees.
s: (a) Angle of reflection 42 degrees
(b) Angle between the beams 84 degrees
(c) No: the reflected ray stays in the plane of the incident ray and normal; the bent part is a new plane
(d) Finds i = 32 degrees and decides to decrease it by 10 degrees

questions.q: Which of these is a use of concentrated sunlight given in the chapter?
questions.a: Melting steel in a solar furnace
o: Melting steel in a solar furnace
Showing the traffic behind a vehicle
Making small print look bigger
Watching a large area of a store

questions.q:
Read these statements.
I. When parallel beams of light fall on a plane mirror, the reflected beams are also parallel.
II. A concave mirror makes parallel beams converge because the rays striking it do not obey the laws of reflection.
III. Solar furnaces, which use concentrated sunlight, are even used for melting steel.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A concave mirror held facing the Sun can make a sheet of paper smoke.
Reason (R): The laws of reflection are valid for all kinds of mirrors.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A mirror is hidden inside a box with a narrow opening. Five parallel beams of light from a torch and comb enter the opening and are reflected back out onto a sheet of white paper (illustrative readings). The gap between neighbouring reflected beams is 8 mm close to the box and 3 mm farther away from it. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: It is a concave mirror, because the reflected beams converge
o: It is a concave mirror, because the reflected beams converge
It is a convex mirror, because the reflected beams converge
It is a convex mirror, because the reflected beams diverge
It is a plane mirror, because five beams still come out

questions.q: (a) What does it mean to say that reflected beams of light 'converge'? (b) Which spherical mirror makes parallel beams of light converge?
questions.a: (a) The reflected beams get closer together. (b) A concave mirror.
s: States that converging beams get closer together
Names the concave mirror

questions.q: Asif wants to show his younger sister how a concave mirror can make paper smoke in sunlight. (a) Write two safety rules from the chapter that he must follow. (b) Asif plans to do it alone on the terrace while his parents are out. Which rule does this break, and why does that rule matter here?
questions.a: (a) Any two: do it only under the supervision of a teacher or an adult; do not look towards the Sun or into the mirror reflecting it; focus the reflected light only on paper, never towards anyone's face or eyes. (b) It breaks the rule that the activity must be done under the supervision of a teacher or adult. It matters because the light concentrated by the mirror produces enough heat to set paper on fire and can harm the eyes.
s: (a) Gives two correct safety rules from the chapter
(b) Names the adult-supervision rule and links it to the heat of the concentrated light

questions.q: Gauri writes in her notes: 'Solar concentrators use only mirrors, and the only thing they are used for is cooking.' Check both parts of her note and correct it.
questions.a: Her note is wrong on both counts. Solar concentrators are devices that concentrate sunlight into a small area using mirrors and lenses, not only mirrors. Cooking is not their only use: the concentrated sunlight heats a liquid to make steam that can generate electricity, and it gives heat for large-scale cooking and for solar furnaces, which can even melt steel.
s: Corrects the first part: solar concentrators use mirrors and lenses
Corrects the second part with another use: steam to generate electricity
Adds a further use or the working idea: solar furnaces (melting steel), sunlight concentrated into a small area

questions.q:
At a science fair in Bikaner, a Class 8 team shows how sunlight can melt wax. Their model has a large curved mirror, about 1 metre across, whose shiny reflecting surface curves inwards. A small metal cup of wax is held on a stand in front of the mirror. When the Sun is out, the mirror sends the sunlight falling on it onto a small bright spot on the cup, and the wax melts in about 3 minutes. When a cloud covers the Sun, the wax stops melting.
(a) What type of mirror does the model use?
(b) What does this mirror do to the parallel rays of sunlight that fall on it?
(c) Why does the wax in the cup melt?
(d) Name one use of concentrated sunlight given in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A concave mirror. (b) It converges them: the reflected rays come closer together. (c) The sunlight collected by the mirror is concentrated on a small spot on the cup, and this produces enough heat there to melt the wax. (d) Any one: heating a liquid to make steam that can generate electricity, large-scale cooking, or solar furnaces (even for melting steel).
s: (a) Names the concave mirror
(b) It converges the parallel rays
(c) The light is concentrated on a small spot, producing heat
(d) Gives one use from the chapter

questions.q: For a science exhibition, Tara builds a model solar power plant. A shiny mirror whose reflecting surface bulges outwards faces the Sun, and a thin black tube of water is fixed in front of it. The plan is to turn the water into steam to run a tiny generator, but after an hour the water is only slightly warm. Her friend says: 'The generator must be faulty.' (a) Name Tara's mirror and say what it does to the parallel rays of sunlight. (b) Explain why the water did not get hot enough. (c) Which mirror should she use instead, and where should she place the tube? (d) Is her friend's explanation correct? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) A convex mirror. It makes the reflected rays spread out (diverge). (b) Because the light is spread over a larger area, it is not concentrated on the tube, so it does not produce enough heat to boil the water into steam. (c) A concave mirror, which converges the sunlight; the tube should be placed at the small bright spot where the reflected light is concentrated. (d) No. The water never became hot enough to make steam, so there was no steam to run the generator; the fault is the choice of mirror, not the generator.
s: (a) Convex mirror; it diverges the parallel rays
(b) The light is spread out, not concentrated, so too little heat reaches the tube
(c) Use a concave mirror and place the tube at its small bright spot
(d) Friend is wrong: no steam was made, so the mirror, not the generator, is the problem

questions.q: Using a torch and a comb with seven openings uncovered, Kavya sends parallel beams onto three mirrors, X, Y and Z, one at a time, and follows the reflected beams on a long sheet of paper (illustrative readings). X: the seven reflected beams stay the same distance apart all along the sheet. Y: the reflected beams come closer and meet at one small spot 15 cm in front of the mirror. Z: the reflected beams spread farther apart and never meet. Her teacher then gives her a fourth mirror, W, whose reflected beams meet at a spot 35 cm in front of it. (a) Identify X, Y and Z. (b) Explain why mirror Z cannot be used to make paper smoke in sunlight. (c) Her paper holder can keep a sheet steady at most 25 cm from a mirror. Decide whether she should use Y or W with this holder, showing your reasoning. (d) For the mirror you chose, where should she hold the paper, and why there? (e) Each ray striking Y obeys the laws of reflection. Why, then, do the reflected beams not stay parallel as they do for X?
questions.a: (a) X is a plane mirror (the reflected beams stay parallel), Y is a concave mirror (the beams converge) and Z is a convex mirror (the beams diverge). (b) Z spreads the light over a larger area instead of concentrating it, so no spot gets enough heat to ignite the paper. (c) Y. Its beams meet 15 cm in front of it, which is within the holder's 25 cm reach; W's beams meet 35 cm away, which is 10 cm beyond the holder's reach. (d) About 15 cm in front of Y, adjusted until there is a sharp bright spot, because there the reflected sunlight is concentrated into a small area and produces enough heat to ignite the paper. (e) Y's reflecting surface is curved (concave). Even though each ray obeys the laws of reflection, the curved surface makes the parallel beams converge on reflection; a plane mirror's flat surface keeps them parallel.
s: (a) X plane, Y concave, Z convex
(b) Z diverges the light, so it is not concentrated enough to ignite the paper
(c) Chooses Y: 15 cm is within 25 cm, while W's 35 cm is beyond the holder
(d) Paper about 15 cm from Y, at the sharp bright spot where the light is concentrated
(e) The curved surface makes the reflected beams converge even though each ray obeys the laws

o: A convex lens, which is thicker at the middle than at the edges
A concave lens, which is thicker at the edges than at the middle
A convex lens, which is thicker at the edges than at the middle
A concave lens, which is thicker at the middle than at the edges

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.

questions.q: True or false? 'An object seen through a concave lens looks upside down once it is far enough away from the lens.' Give a reason or write the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. An object seen through a concave lens always appears erect and diminished; only its size changes with distance. It is through a convex lens that a farther object appears inverted.

Corrects it: through a concave lens the object always looks erect and diminished

questions.q: A clear glass piece with curved surfaces is 4.5 mm thick at its middle and 1.5 mm thick at its edges. (a) Name this lens and give the reason from its shape. (b) Describe how a flower held just behind it and a building far away would look through it.
questions.a: (a) A convex lens, because it is thicker at the middle (4.5 mm) than at the edges (1.5 mm). (b) The near flower would look erect and enlarged; the far building would look inverted (and smaller).
s: (a) Names a convex lens because the middle is thicker than the edges
(b) Near flower erect and enlarged, far building inverted

questions.q: Nandini says: 'A flat glass window pane is not a lens, even though it is a piece of transparent glass.' Is she right? Give two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. A lens is a piece of transparent material that has curved surfaces, and a window pane is flat. Also, objects seen through a flat window pane all look the same size and shape, while a curved lens changes how big objects look (a convex lens can make them look enlarged, a concave lens makes them look diminished).
s: Verdict: she is right
A lens must have curved surfaces; the pane is flat
Through the pane objects keep the same size and shape, unlike through a lens

questions.q: A device is one of these five: a plane mirror, a concave mirror, a convex mirror, a convex lens or a concave lens. Meher records (illustrative): a toy 3 cm away looks erect and smaller than it is; the same toy 50 cm away looks erect and smaller still; and the toy and her eye were on opposite sides of the device. Use all three records to decide which device it is, ruling out the other four, and then predict what the device does to a parallel beam of light.
questions.a: Step 1: The image of a close toy is diminished, so it cannot be a plane mirror (same size) or a concave mirror or convex lens (both show a close object erect and enlarged); the image also stays erect when the toy is far, which fits only a convex mirror or a concave lens. Step 2: The toy and her eye were on opposite sides, so she was seeing through the device: it lets light pass, so it is a lens, not a mirror. It is therefore a concave lens. Step 3: A concave lens is a diverging lens, so it makes a parallel beam of light spread out.
s: Rules out plane mirror (same size), concave mirror and convex lens (enlarged when close), leaving convex mirror or concave lens
Opposite sides means she saw through it, so it is a lens: a concave lens
Predicts that it diverges (spreads out) a parallel beam

questions.q:
Thatha in Madurai wants to read the tiny print on a temple calendar. In his drawer he finds three clear glass pieces. Piece P is flat on both sides. Piece Q has curved surfaces and is 4 mm thick at the middle and 1 mm thick at the edges. Piece R has curved surfaces and is 3 mm thick at the edges and 1 mm thick at the middle. He holds each piece 2 cm above the print and looks down through it. (He also notices that when Q is lifted more than about 10 cm above the print, the letters through it look upside down.)
(a) Name pieces Q and R.
(b) Through which piece will the letters look erect and bigger?
(c) Through which piece will the letters look the same size?
(d) His grandson says: 'Lift piece Q to 40 cm above the calendar and the letters will get bigger still.' Is this good advice? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Q is a convex lens (thicker at the middle); R is a concave lens (thicker at the edges). (b) Piece Q, the convex lens, held close to the print. (c) Piece P, the flat glass, through which things keep their size and shape. (d) No. As the distance between the print and a convex lens increases, the letters appear inverted; they are enlarged at first and then become smaller. So Thatha should keep Q close to the print, where the letters look erect and enlarged.
s: (a) Q convex lens, R concave lens
(b) Piece Q held close
(c) Piece P, the flat glass
(d) No: farther away the letters turn inverted and then shrink, so keep Q close

questions.q: Reena says: 'A concave mirror and a convex lens change the image with distance in the same way, and both of them reflect light back towards us.' Compare the two under these heads and then judge her statement. (a) What does each do with the light that falls on it? (b) The image of a small object placed very close. (c) The image as the object is moved farther away. (d) What the shape of each looks like. (e) Is Reena right, wrong or partly right? Justify using (a) to (d).
questions.a: (a) A concave mirror reflects the light back; a convex lens lets light pass through it, so we see the image in the mirror but see things through the lens. (b) Both give an erect, enlarged image of a very close object. (c) For both, the image becomes inverted as the object moves away, at first enlarged and then getting smaller. (d) The concave mirror has a reflecting surface that curves inwards; the convex lens is thicker at the middle than at the edges. (e) Partly right. The first part is right: by (b) and (c), the image changes with distance in the same way for both. The second part is wrong: by (a), only the mirror reflects light back; the lens lets light pass through it.
s: (a) Mirror reflects light; lens lets light pass through
(b) Both erect and enlarged when the object is close
(c) Both become inverted farther away, enlarged first and then smaller
(d) Mirror's reflecting surface curves inwards; lens is thicker in the middle
(e) Partly right: same change with distance is right, but only the mirror reflects; the lens lets light through

questions.q: (a) Why is a convex lens also called a converging lens? (b) Name one device, other than eyeglasses, that uses lenses to work.
questions.a: (a) Because it makes a parallel beam of light passing through it converge, that is, come closer together. (b) Any one: a camera, a telescope or a microscope.
s: (a) A convex lens converges (brings together) the light passing through it
(b) Names a camera, telescope or microscope

questions.q: (a) A band of parallel light beams 5 cm wide passes through a lens, and on a sheet of paper a short distance beyond the lens the band is only 2 cm wide. Name the lens. (b) If this lens is replaced by a concave lens, will the band on the same sheet be wider or narrower than 5 cm? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) A convex lens, because the beams have come closer together (converged), from 5 cm to 2 cm. (b) Wider than 5 cm, because a concave lens is a diverging lens: it makes the beams spread apart.
s: (a) Names a convex lens from the narrowing of the band
(b) Wider than 5 cm, because a concave lens diverges the beams

questions.q: Lata says: 'Lenses are used in cameras, telescopes and microscopes, but there is no lens anywhere inside the human body.' Is she right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that cameras, telescopes and microscopes all use lenses to work. But she is wrong about the body: our eye has a convex lens inside it, and this lens can change its shape, which is what lets us read a book and also see something far away.
s: Verdict partly right; agrees that cameras, telescopes and microscopes use lenses
Corrects her: the eye has a convex lens inside it
The eye's lens can change shape, letting us see near and far

questions.q:
A women's self-help group in Kutch wants to heat water with sunlight. They test two small solar concentrators of the same width. Device M uses a concave mirror; Device L uses a convex lens. In tests, each brought sunlight to a small bright spot, and the water heated well only when the pot's base was right at that spot. Each device, of either kind, heats 10 litres of water a day. Device M costs Rs 700 and Device L costs Rs 900. The group has Rs 4,000 and needs 50 litres of hot water a day.
(a) What does each device do to the parallel rays of sunlight?
(b) Why did the water heat well only when the pot was at the bright spot?
(c) Give one safety rule the women must follow while adjusting either device.
(d) Which device should the group buy? Justify with the costs and the litres of water.
questions.a: (a) Both converge the parallel rays: the concave mirror by reflecting them, the convex lens as they pass through it. (b) At the bright spot the sunlight is concentrated into a small area, which produces enough heat there; away from the spot the same light is spread over a larger area. (c) Any one: do not look at the Sun directly, into the mirror or through the lens; work under adult supervision; never point the bright spot towards anyone's face or eyes. (d) Device M. Rs 4,000 buys 5 mirrors (5 x 700 = Rs 3,500), which heat 5 x 10 = 50 litres a day, meeting the need. It buys only 4 lenses (4 x 900 = Rs 3,600; a fifth would make Rs 4,500), which heat 40 litres, 10 litres short.
s: (a) Both converge the rays; mirror by reflection, lens as light passes through
(b) Light is concentrated into a small area at the spot, producing enough heat
(c) Gives one correct safety rule
(d) Chooses M: 5 mirrors for Rs 3,500 give 50 litres; only 4 lenses fit, giving 40 litres

questions.q: Before a test, Rohit wrote four revision lines. Check each line, say whether it is correct, and correct any wrong one. Line 1: A convex lens converges a light beam, while a concave lens diverges it. Line 2: An object seen through a concave lens looks enlarged when it is close to the lens. Line 3: A parallel beam passes through a thin transparent glass plate as it is. Line 4: The lens inside our eye is a convex lens whose shape cannot change.
questions.a: Line 1 is correct. Line 2 is wrong: an object seen through a concave lens always appears erect and diminished. Line 3 is correct. Line 4 is wrong: the eye's lens is convex, but it can change its shape, which is what lets us read a book and also see something far away.
s: Line 1 judged correct
Line 2 corrected: a concave lens always gives an erect, diminished view
Line 3 judged correct
Line 4 corrected: the eye's convex lens can change its shape

questions.q: Vikram and Asha each test an unlabelled lens three ways. Vikram's lens: Test 1, parallel beams passed through it come closer together; Test 2, print 1 cm under it looks erect and larger; Test 3, a building 50 m away looks inverted. Asha's lens: Test 1, parallel beams spread apart; Test 2, print 1 cm under it looks erect and smaller; Test 3, the building looks erect and smaller. (a) Identify Vikram's lens, using two of his tests. (b) Identify Asha's lens, using two of her tests. (c) Which of the two lenses is thicker at the middle than at the edges? (d) Which lens could be used to burn paper with sunlight, and why? (e) Asha says: 'To tell these two lenses apart, any one of the three tests would have been enough.' Is she right? Justify.
questions.a: (a) A convex lens: it converges the beams (Test 1), and it shows near print erect and enlarged (Test 2) while a far building looks inverted (Test 3). (b) A concave lens: it diverges the beams (Test 1), and it shows objects erect and diminished at every distance (Tests 2 and 3). (c) Vikram's convex lens. (d) Vikram's convex lens, because it converges sunlight into a small area, producing enough heat to burn paper. (e) Yes. In every test the two lenses gave opposite results: converging against diverging beams, enlarged against diminished near print, and inverted against erect far building. So any one test separates a convex lens from a concave lens.
s: (a) Convex lens, backed by two of Vikram's tests
(b) Concave lens, backed by two of Asha's tests
(c) Vikram's convex lens is thicker at the middle
(d) Vikram's lens, because it converges and concentrates sunlight
(e) Yes: each test gives opposite results for the two lenses
